worst_places.after:
All three reduce the rate, but each hands you a different value out of the burst.

```
source           -a-b-c---------d-e-------|
debounceTime(4)  ---------c---------e-----|  last value after a pause
throttleTime(4)  -a-------------d---------|  first value, then silence
auditTime(4)     -----c-------------e-----|  last value of the window
```

`debounceTime` waits for a pause and emits the **last** value. That is search-as-you-type. `throttleTime` emits the **first** value at once, then stays silent for the window. That is scroll, button protection, analytics. `auditTime` waits out the window and emits the **last** value from it — "no more often, but always current". Two questions decide: must the reaction be immediate, and which value of the series do you need? (The same three operators are covered in depth in [Transformation and Filtering Operators].)

worst_places.quote: Three mandatory elements: a **limit** (`retry()` without `count` repeats forever), a **delay**, preferably growing (`delay: (err, n) => timer(500 * 2 ** (n - 1))` — instant repeats finish off a downed service and earn a rate-limit ban), and a **filter by error type**: retry `5xx`, timeouts and `status === 0`, but retrying `401`/`422` is pointless because the result will not change.
worst_places.problem: A 59-word sentence carrying three separate rules, each with its own parenthetical, plus a code expression embedded mid-clause. By the time the reader reaches "and a **filter by error type**" they have lost the "Three mandatory elements" frame. 45 of the 199 sentences in this file (22.6%) are over the 25-word EN limit, against 7.4% in the `ru` twin — this is the sharpest RU/EN gap in the zone.
worst_places.before: Three mandatory elements: a **limit** (`retry()` without `count` repeats forever), a **delay**, preferably growing (`delay: (err, n) => timer(500 * 2 ** (n - 1))` — instant repeats finish off a downed service and earn a rate-limit ban), and a **filter by error type**: retry `5xx`, timeouts and `status === 0`, but retrying `401`/`422` is pointless because the result will not change.
worst_places.after:
Three elements are mandatory.

**A limit.** `retry()` without `count` repeats forever.

**A delay, preferably a growing one**: `delay: (err, n) => timer(500 * 2 ** (n - 1))`. Instant repeats hit a service that is already down, and the server may block you for exceeding its request limit.

**A filter by error type.** Retry `5xx`, timeouts and `status === 0`. Retrying `401` or `422` is pointless: the result will not change.

worst_places.quote: **A delay, preferably growing.** Instant repeats against a downed service are a way to finish it off and earn a rate-limit ban.
worst_places.problem: Three idioms in one 22-word sentence: "a downed service" (adjectival past participle of a phrasal verb), "finish it off" (phrasal verb, figurative), "earn a ... ban" (metaphorical use of earn). A B1-B2 reader can decode each word and still miss that the sentence means "you will make the outage worse and get blocked". The same file also uses "the crux", "folds it into ordinary error handling", "surfaces a meaningful error" and "hand-rolled backoff"; the `ru` twin is plain throughout.
worst_places.before: **A delay, preferably growing.** Instant repeats against a downed service are a way to finish it off and earn a rate-limit ban.
worst_places.after: **A delay, preferably a growing one.** If a service is already failing, retrying instantly makes the outage worse — and many servers block a client that sends too many requests per second.

worst_places.quote: What is wrong: nobody closes the inner subscriptions (they pile up as `:id` changes quickly); previous requests are not cancelled, so a response for an old ticket may land on screen; an error at any level breaks the whole construct with no single place to handle it; and unsubscribing is impossible — the outer teardown does not stop the inner ones.
worst_places.problem: 60 words and four independent failure modes chained with semicolons. The article's own interview-trap section later says a good answer "names four concrete consequences" — so the four are load-bearing and the reader is meant to memorize them, but the format (one run-on sentence) is the hardest possible way to memorize four items. worst_places.before: What is wrong: nobody closes the inner subscriptions (they pile up as `:id` changes quickly); previous requests are not cancelled, so a response for an old ticket may land on screen; an error at any level breaks the whole construct with no single place to handle it; and unsubscribing is impossible — the outer teardown does not stop the inner ones.
worst_places.after:
Four things are wrong here:

1. **Nobody closes the inner subscriptions.** They pile up as `:id` changes quickly.
2. **Previous requests are not cancelled.** A response for an old ticket may land on screen.
3. **An error at any level breaks the whole construct**, and there is no single place to handle it.
4. **Unsubscribing is impossible.** The outer teardown does not stop the inner ones.

worst_places.after:
## share и shareReplay

`share()` вставляет между источником и подписчиками `Subject`: первая подписка запускает источник, остальные присоединяются к тому же результату. Когда подписчиков не остаётся, источник отписывается — и следующая подписка запустит работу заново. `shareReplay(bufferSize)` делает то же, но с буфером: поздний подписчик немедленно получает последние N значений.

Разница между четырьмя формами вызова — в том, что происходит, когда подписчиков не осталось:

```
        share и shareReplay: что выбрать
┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
│ вызов                    │ риск                │
...
```

patterns: The English version is systematically harder than the Russian one, and by far more than the usual ~19% expansion. Over-limit sentences: en/04 14.4% vs ru/04 1.1%; en/06 16.0% vs ru/06 6.2%; en/08 22.6% vs ru/08 7.4%; en/01 14.9% vs ru/01 2.7%. The cause is visible sentence by sentence: where the Russian splits a rule into two short sentences or a bullet, the English joins them with a semicolon or an em-dash and adds a parenthetical. On top of that the English reaches for idiom where the Russian is plain — "the tell", "a downed service", "finish it off", "in promise-land", "the crux", "stumps you", "a straight-up bug", "unrolls anything iterable", "waits out the window", "picks up the destruction context". Every one of these has a plain B1-B2 equivalent and the Russian already uses it. F is the lowest-scoring criterion in the zone (2.9) while G is the highest (4.3).

Every article carries exactly one wide box-drawing decision table (99-123 characters), and in three articles that table is the FIRST thing under its heading, before any prose defines the thing being tabulated (ru/02 «Откуда берутся потоки», ru/07 «share и shareReplay», ru/06 «finalize» — where the table actually summarises all eight error operators, not finalize). The marble diagrams themselves are fine at 65-85 characters and their annotation lines, not the marbles, drive that width; the box tables are the mobile problem. Fix is mechanical and does not touch content: move the lead sentence above the table, and split the widest column out into a list under the diagram.
notes: Marble-diagram verdict: the notation is taught properly (art. 03 «Как читать marble-диаграмму»), and every diagram before it carries its own inline legend, so nothing is assumed — but the formal lesson sits in file 3 of 8 while files 1 and 2 already use the notation. Coverage is uneven: the four flattening operators (04) and combineLatest/withLatestFrom/forkJoin/zip (05) get first-class diagrams, while merge, concat, race, startWith (05), scan vs reduce (03), take/distinctUntilChanged (03), timeout and finalize (06) and takeUntil ordering (07) get prose only — and `concat`'s infinite-first-source trap in particular would be self-evident on one marble line. Article 08 has zero diagrams across 79 paragraphs. On the operator-choice question the zone is genuinely strong: 04 gives a three-question selection algorithm plus a "cost of getting it wrong" column, 05 opens with three questions, 03 ends every time-operator with a plain-words criterion — this is the best-executed part of the zone and should be the model for other topics. Widths measured: box tables ru 104-118 / en 99-123 chars; marble diagrams ru 65-84 / en 68-85.
